How is Montana divided into counties and cities?

Montana has 56 counties, and nearly every step of a house sale runs through one of them. Populations range from 548 people in Petroleum County to 172,692 in Yellowstone County, according to the list of Montana counties on Wikipedia.

Two places work differently from the rest. Butte and Silver Bow County are one consolidated city-county, and so are Anaconda and Deer Lodge County. If your house is in Butte, the county and city offices you deal with are tied together. Our Butte page covers that local picture.

These county seats match the cities we work in most:

  • Billings: Yellowstone County
  • Missoula: Missoula County
  • Great Falls: Cascade County
  • Bozeman: Gallatin County
  • Helena: Lewis and Clark County
  • Kalispell: Flathead County

Knowing the county matters because the treasurer, the clerk and recorder, and the district court that touch your sale all sit at that level.

Who do you call about property tax and recording when you sell a Montana house?

Call the county treasurer for the tax bill and the county clerk and recorder for the deed. Montana sets the payment calendar in statute: under MCA 15-16-102, half of the tax is due by 5 p.m. on November 30, or within 30 days after the tax notice is postmarked if that is later, and the other half by 5 p.m. on May 31.

Late payment is costly. Unpaid amounts draw interest at 5/6 of 1 percent a month, and a 2 percent penalty is added. A taxpayer may pay the current year without clearing older delinquent taxes, but the county treasurer applies any payment toward the oldest delinquency first.

When a deed is recorded, the clerk and recorder must receive a realty transfer certificate stating the price paid. MCA 15-7-305 says the instrument cannot be accepted for recording until the certificate arrives. Ask the clerk and recorder for current recording fees.

Several of our guides go deeper on the money side. Start with the Montana property tax guide or a county guide such as the one for Yellowstone County or Flathead County.

How does foreclosure work in Montana, and how long does it take?

Most Montana home loans use a trust indenture, and those are foreclosed by advertisement and sale rather than through a court case. The rules sit in the Small Tract Financing part of the code, and MCA 71-1-315 lays out the notice steps.

The minimum timeline starts with the recorded notice of sale. These are the required pieces:

  • At least 120 days before the sale date, a copy of the notice goes by certified mail to the borrower and other listed parties.
  • At least 20 days before the sale, a copy is posted in a conspicuous place on the property.
  • The notice is published once a week for three successive weeks in a newspaper.
  • Affidavits of mailing, posting and publication must be recorded on or before the sale date.

The sale is a public auction to the highest bidder, and the buyer pays cash. The trustee may postpone it for up to 15 days. If a bankruptcy stay or court order blocks the sale, postponements are allowed in blocks of up to 30 days, with a total cap of 120 days.

One more rule helps borrowers. When a trust indenture is foreclosed this way, MCA 71-1-317 bars a deficiency judgment against the borrower or guarantor. That does not erase the lost equity, which is why many owners sell before the auction date. Read our Montana guides by city and county for the next steps, and talk to a Montana attorney about your own loan documents.

What happens to an inherited house in Montana probate?

Montana has adopted the Uniform Probate Code, and the MSU Extension guide republished by Montana Law Help says that makes probate lighter than in states without it. A house passes through probate unless it was held in a trust or in joint tenancy with right of survivorship.

The process runs through the district court in the county where the person lived. An application for informal probate can go to the clerk of the district court no sooner than 120 hours after the death. Creditors get four months after the first newspaper notice to file claims, and the guide says a formal closing is possible six months after appointment once that window has passed.

Timing varies. The same guide says some probates finish within six months and that a formal proceeding typically takes about ten months. Smaller estates have shortcuts: an affidavit may collect personal property 30 days after death when the estate is $50,000 or less, and a small estate summary procedure exists for the smallest estates.

Probate stepMontana timing
Earliest informal application120 hours after death
Notice to heirs and deviseesWithin 30 days of appointment
Creditor claim periodFour months after first publication
Typical formal probateAbout ten months

Whoever is appointed as personal representative signs for the estate, so a buyer will want to see that appointment before closing. Our Montana probate guide walks through selling the house, and the estate and inheritance tax page covers what heirs owe.

How do homestead rules affect a Montana sale?

Montana uses the word homestead for two separate things, and mixing them up causes trouble at closing. One is a homestead declaration, which protects equity from creditors. The other is the Homestead Reduced Rate, a property tax program run by the Department of Revenue.

On the declaration side, MCA 70-32-104 caps the value. The limit was $350,000 in 2021 and rises by 4 percent each calendar year after that, so the current number is higher than the starting figure. An owner of an undivided interest is limited to a share in proportion to that interest.

On the tax side, the Department of Revenue says enrollment for the 2026 tax year closed March 20, 2026, and its FAQ page now covers the 2027 enrollment period. The same page has a question for owners who are selling an enrolled home, so check it before you list or accept an offer. If you are unsure which program applies to your house, call your county assessor or the Department of Revenue. Our Montana homestead guide explains both in more detail.

What if a Montana house has tenants?

Tenants stay in place during a sale unless the lease or the law says otherwise, so read the lease first. For month-to-month tenancies under the Residential Landlord and Tenant Act, MCA 70-24-441 lets either side end the tenancy with at least 30 days' written notice. A week-to-week tenancy needs 7 days.

A separate statute, MCA 70-26-109, lets a landlord change the terms of a month-to-month lease by written notice given at least 15 days before the end of the month. It changes rent and terms and does not end a tenancy.

Fixed-term leases are different, and the buyer usually takes the property subject to them. Give the buyer copies of every lease and notice early. Our Montana landlord tenant guide covers selling a rental in detail.

What does a cash as-is sale look like in Montana?

An as-is cash sale means the buyer takes the house in its current condition and does not ask the seller to repair it first. The sale still follows normal steps: a purchase agreement, a title search, a deed signed before a notary, a realty transfer certificate, and recording with the county clerk and recorder.

Those steps can move fast when the title is clean. They slow down when the file has an unpaid tax bill, an open probate, a lien or a co-owner who has not signed. A quitclaim deed passes only what the signer owns, so a buyer will want to know who really holds title. See our quitclaim deed page for how that works.

Who handles closing varies by county and by deal, so ask the title or escrow office you plan to use how it works and what it charges.

What property issues come up when selling in Montana?

Radon is the one with an official state program behind it. The Montana Department of Environmental Quality runs a Radon Control Program created under the Radon Control Act of 1993. It operates a toll-free hotline at 1-800-546-0483 and distributes subsidized test kits to residents.

A buyer may ask for a radon test during inspection. The DEQ lists radon service providers and says it does not certify or vouch for them, so gather several written bids and check references before hiring anyone.

For well and septic systems, flood risk or wildfire exposure, ask your county sanitarian or planning office what applies to your parcel.

Frequently asked questions

How many counties does Montana have?

Montana has 56 counties. Butte and Silver Bow County, and Anaconda and Deer Lodge County, are consolidated city-counties.

When are Montana property taxes due?

Half is due by 5 p.m. on November 30 (or 30 days after the notice is postmarked, if later) and half by 5 p.m. on May 31. Late amounts draw interest of 5/6 of 1 percent a month plus a 2 percent penalty.

Is foreclosure in Montana handled by a court?

Most loans use a trust indenture and are foreclosed by advertisement and sale. Notice must be mailed by certified mail at least 120 days before the sale, with posting and three weeks of publication.

Can a lender sue me for the rest of the loan after a trustee sale?

For a trust indenture foreclosed by advertisement and sale, MCA 71-1-317 bars a deficiency judgment against the borrower or guarantor.

How long does probate take in Montana?

Some probates finish within six months, and a formal proceeding typically takes about ten months, according to the MSU Extension guide.

How much notice ends a month-to-month tenancy?

Under MCA 70-24-441, either side may end a month-to-month tenancy with at least 30 days of written notice.

Does a deed need anything besides a signature to be recorded?

The county clerk and recorder must receive a realty transfer certificate before it accepts the deed for recording.

Can I sell a house that needs repairs?

Yes. An as-is sale means the buyer takes the house in its current condition, so you do not need to fix it first.
